extracted.intended_audience: science/medical press officers, science journalists, and researchers in science communication
extracted.subtask_description: Coding and analysis protocol for evaluating health- and biomedical-related press releases (and their associated journal articles and news stories) for exaggeration, caveats, justifications, advice, and related framing; and measuring associations with news uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration (operational definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration was defined as claims or advice in press releases or news that were coded at a level above any of the associated statements in the peer-reviewed journal article (i.e. message creep beyond the journal article text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition uses the journal article as the baseline (not an independent truth standard). Example: when news makes a causal claim but the journal article did not, that counts as exaggeration. Note that this will not identify exaggeration already present in the journal article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice level
rubrics_metrics.description: Each source was coded for the maximum level of advice using four categories: no advice; implicit advice; explicit advice but not to the reader/general public; explicit advice to the reader or general public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: implicit ('for adults with a BMI greater than 35 kg/m2…'); explicit but not to reader ('clinicians must exercise caution…'); explicit to reader ('patients … should consider starting statin treatment'). Inclusion for analysis required at least one source in the trio to contain implicit or explicit advice. Used to detect exaggeration when press release/news advice is stronger than the journal article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal claim strength (7-level scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Main statements of findings were coded according to seven levels: no statement, statement of no relationship, correlational, ambiguous, conditional causal, can cause, and causal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coding was applied to the title and first two sentences of press releases and news (and to abstract and discussion in journal articles) because main claims are typically front-loaded. Analyses focused on correlational cross-sectional and longitudinal studies (excluded interventions, qualitative, simulation designs). Exaggeration occurs when the press release/news has a stronger causal level than the journal article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human inference from non-human research
rubrics_metrics.description: For journal articles based on non-human samples (animals, cells, simulations), press releases and news were coded as: explicitly non-human, implicitly human, or explicitly human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to detect inappropriate generalisation to humans. Low sample sizes limited some analyses; partial results reported separately. Example concern: claiming human relevance when the study was non-human.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Coded presence or absence of caveats for causal/correlational statements and for explicit advice in press releases and news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat examples: 'We still need more research to clarify whether vitamin D directly prevents bowel cancer…'. Caveats were rare (~14–15%) but when present were often placed at the end of press releases; caveats in press releases strongly increased odds of caveats appearing in subsequent news and did not reduce likelihood of news uptake (reported odds ratios and CIs). Analyses combined journal and university press release datasets when necessary to increase N.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of justifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Coded whether press releases (and news) contained justifications for causal statements or explicit advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justifications were operationalised as explicit reasons or context given to support the strength of a claim (e.g. methodological caveats, sampling notes). Rates were reported separately for advice and causal statements; presence of justifications in press releases greatly increased odds of justifications appearing in news.

rubrics_metrics.name: News uptake (binary and count)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured whether a press release had at least one resulting news story (binary news uptake) and the number of news stories per press release (count).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals and inferential tests to compare uptake between press releases with/without exaggeration, caveats, or justifications. Finding: exaggeration did not increase news uptake and caveats did not decrease it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location for coding main claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Main claims were coded from specific article locations: for news and press releases the title and first two sentences; for journal articles the abstract and discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: main claims are usually front-loaded and therefore have the largest influence on readers. This coding rule focuses the measure on headline/main-message framing rather than subordinate text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling and inclusion criteria for press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases were included if they were based on research with possible relevance to human health, psychology, or neuroscience and originated from selected leading journals (Lancet, BMJ, Science, Nature family journals) during 2011.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases were collected from journal pages, EurekAlert, or press sites; news stories were identified from Nexis, BBC, Reuters, and Google. Note limitation: not all journals issue press releases (e.g., NEJM), and the sampled journals/settings limit generalisability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding instrument breadth and effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Coding used a structured sheet of 191 questions applied to each press release/journal article/news set; coding took ~3–4 hours per set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High reliability standard: a random subset (27.5% of press releases) was double-coded yielding 98.3% concordance and κ = 0.97. Where concordance is high, increasing sample size may be preferable to more double-coding for reliability of estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic treatment of clustering and uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical analyses accounted for clustering (multiple news stories per press release) using generalized estimating equations to estimate percentages, 95% CIs, and odds ratios; bootstrapping used for news uptake comparisons without clustering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a methodological rubric for evaluating association metrics (e.g., odds ratios for association between press release exaggeration and news exaggeration). Reporting should include confidence intervals and account for clustered observations where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of baseline (journal article) as reference standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons judged exaggeration relative to the associated peer-reviewed journal article rather than an external objective truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note that if journal articles themselves contain exaggeration relative to underlying results/expert consensus, the study will undercount total exaggeration; this limitation should be acknowledged when using this rubric.
